questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A toy, of mass 0.22 kg, is released from rest on a smooth curved surface as shown. [Diagram: toy at the top of a smooth curved ramp, 40 cm above the flat bottom; the ramp levels out and leads to a horizontal spring fixed at the end.] It slides down the curved surface through a vertical distance of 40 cm and strikes a spring of force constant $350\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$, and compresses it a distance $x$ before coming to rest momentarily. Assuming no energy loss, what is the value of $x$? A $4.9\times10^{-3}$ m B $7.2\times10^{-3}$ m C $2.2\times10^{-2}$ m D $7.0\times10^{-2}$ m

stemImage.alt: Question 4: A toy, of mass 0.22 kg, is released from rest on a smooth curved surface as shown. It slides down the curved surface through a vertical distance of 40 cm and st

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Single energy-conservation equation linking GPE to elastic PE.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square-root or forgetting the factor of 1/2 in elastic PE

explanation.body:
By conservation of energy, loss in GPE = gain in elastic potential energy:

$mgh = \tfrac{1}{2}kx^2$, so $x = \sqrt{\dfrac{2mgh}{k}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2(0.22)(9.81)(0.40)}{350}} = 7.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: This is $x^2$: forgets to take the square root.
perOption.B: About what you get with $h = 0.40$ cm taken as $0.004$ m (factor-of-100 error in $h$).
perOption.C: Omits $g$ from $mgh$.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An old-fashioned 60 W lamp converts 95% of its energy supply into heat. A 4.0 W modern lamp has the same power output of light as the old-fashioned lamp.

What is the efficiency of the modern lamp?
questions.stemText: An old-fashioned 60 W lamp converts 95% of its energy supply into heat. A 4.0 W modern lamp has the same power output of light as the old-fashioned lamp. What is the efficiency of the modern lamp? A 5.0% B 6.7% C 75% D 95%

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two-step efficiency calculation using useful light power.
questions.misconception: Confusing heat output percentage with efficiency

explanation.body: The old lamp’s useful light output is $60(100-95)/100=3.0\ \mathrm{W}$. The modern lamp produces the same light output with a $4.0\ \mathrm{W}$ input, so its efficiency is $(3.0/4.0)\times100\%=75\%$.

perOption.A: Uses the old lamp’s efficiency.
perOption.B: Divides the modern lamp’s input power by the old lamp’s input power.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the fraction of the old lamp’s input converted to heat.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A driving force of 1.6 kN is produced by the car engine on the wheels to keep the car moving at a constant speed of 11 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ on level road.

The total energy of the fuel consumed by the engine is 1.8 MJ per minute.

What is the efficiency of the car in converting the energy of the fuel into useful work done on the car to keep it moving at the constant speed of 11 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ on level ground?
questions.stemText: A driving force of 1.6 kN is produced by the car engine on the wheels to keep the car moving at a constant speed of 11 m s-1 on level road. The total energy of the fuel consumed by the engine is 1.8 MJ per minute. What is the efficiency of the car in converting the energy of the fuel into useful work done on the car to keep it moving at the constant speed of 11 m s-1 on level ground? A 20 % B 33 % C 36 % D 59 %

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two-step: useful power from P = Fv, then input power from energy per minute.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to convert energy per minute into power

explanation.body: The useful output power is $Fv=1600(11)=17\,600\ \mathrm W$, all of which goes into overcoming resistance at constant speed on level ground. The fuel supplies $1.8\times10^6/60=30\,000\ \mathrm W$. The efficiency is $(17\,600/30\,000)\times100\%\approx59\%$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the ratio of the $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful power to the $30.0\ \mathrm{kW}$ fuel input.
perOption.B: At the stated fuel input, this percentage accounts for only about $10\ \mathrm{kW}$ of useful power.
perOption.C: This percentage treats the roughly $17.6\ \mathrm{kW}$ useful output as only a little over a third of the $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ input.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: The force-extension graph of a spring is as shown. [Graph: straight line through origin; extension $x_1$ corresponds to force $F_1$, extension $x_2$ to force $F_2$.] What is the change in elastic potential energy when the extension of the spring is increased from $x_1$ to $x_2$? A $F_2x_2 - F_1x_1$ B $\frac{1}{2}(F_2x_2 - F_1x_1)$ C $F_2x_2^2 - F_1x_1^2$ D $\frac{1}{2}(F_2x_2^2 - F_1x_1^2)$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: The force-extension graph of a spring is as shown. force F2 F1 0 extension 0 x1 x2 What is the change in elastic potential energy when the extension of the spri

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Area under a linear force–extension graph between two points.
questions.misconception: Using $Fx$ instead of $\tfrac{1}{2}Fx$ for elastic energy

explanation.body: The elastic potential energy is the area under the force–extension graph. The triangular area grows from $\tfrac12F_1x_1$ to $\tfrac12F_2x_2$. The increase is therefore $\tfrac12(F_2x_2-F_1x_1)$.

perOption.A: Uses rectangular areas and misses the factor of one-half.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Squares the extensions and omits the triangular-area factor.
perOption.D: Squares the extensions even though the base of each triangle is the extension itself.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A spring has an unstretched length of $x$. When a mass $m$ is suspended vertically from the end of the spring, the spring extends to a new length of $y$. What is the elastic potential energy stored in the spring? A $\frac{1}{2}mg(y-x)$ B $mg(y-x)$ C $\frac{1}{2}mg(y-x)^2$ D $mg(y-x)^2$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: A spring has an unstretched length of x. When a mass m is suspended vertically from the end of the spring, the spring extends to a new length of y. What is the

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Recall of $E = \tfrac{1}{2}Fx$ with extension $y - x$.
questions.misconception: Equating elastic energy stored to gravitational energy lost by the mass

explanation.body: Assuming Hooke’s law, the force–extension graph is a straight line through the origin, so its triangular area gives stored energy $\tfrac12 Fe$. At equilibrium $F=mg$ and $e=y-x$, so the stored energy is $\tfrac12 mg(y-x)$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the rectangular area under the final force and omits the factor of one-half.
perOption.C: Squares the extension even though the expression already uses the final force.
perOption.D: Squares the extension and omits the triangular-area factor.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A force of 80 N pulls an object of weight 40 N from rest up an incline of 30° through 3.0 m as shown. A frictional force of 30 N acts on the object. [Diagram: block on a 30° incline, 80 N force up the slope parallel to it, 3.0 m displacement up the slope] What are the heat generated due to friction and the gain in kinetic energy of the mass? (heat / J, gain in KE / J) A 210, 0 B 90, 90 C 90, 30 D 210, 240

stemImage.alt: Question 7: A force of 80 N pulls an object of weight 40 N from rest up an incline of 30° through 3.0 m as shown. A frictional force of 30 N acts on the object. 80 N 3.0 m

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Energy bookkeeping with work, friction and GPE on an incline.
questions.misconception: Using the distance along the slope as the vertical height gain

explanation.body: The work done against friction becomes heat, $30(3.0)=90\ \mathrm{J}$. The pulling force does work $80(3.0)=\Delta E_k+40(3.0\sin30^\circ)+90$. Solving gives $\Delta E_k=90\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Overstates the frictional work and assumes the object gains zero kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the full slope distance as the vertical rise, overstating the gravitational energy gain.
perOption.D: Treats all the pulling work as kinetic energy and overstates the heat from friction.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A car of mass 1500 kg travels at constant velocity of 30 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ down a slope. The slope is at an angle of 6.0° to the horizontal, as shown.

The magnitude of the total resistive force acting on the car is 2000 N. What is the power output of the car’s engine?
questions.stemText: A car of mass 1500 kg travels at constant velocity of 30 m s−1 down a slope. The slope is at an angle of 6.0° to the horizontal, as shown. The magnitude of the total resistive force acting on the car is 2000 N. What is the power output of the car’s engine? A 14 kW B 60 kW C 110 kW D 380 kW

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs a force balance on a slope, noting that gravity helps drive the car downhill, before using $P = Fv$.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the component of weight along the slope

explanation.body: Constant velocity means the net force along the slope is zero. The engine force and the downhill component of weight together balance the resistive force, so $F=2000-1500(9.81)\sin6.0^\circ=462\ \mathrm N$. The engine power is $P=Fv=462(30)\approx14\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Correct. Gravity supplies part of the downhill force.
perOption.B: This assigns the full resistive force to the engine and omits gravity’s downhill contribution.
perOption.C: This adds the downhill component of weight to the resistance when solving for the engine force.
perOption.D: This power implies a driving force far above the resistance, even before gravity’s downhill contribution is included.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A motor of power 10 W is used to lift a load of 20 N. The efficiency of the motor is 25 %.

How long does it take to lift the load through a vertical distance of 0.50 m?
questions.stemText: A motor of power 10 W is used to lift a load of 20 N. The efficiency of the motor is 25 %. How long does it take to lift the load through a vertical distance of 0.50 m? A 0.040 s B 0.25 s C 4.0 s D 39 s

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Simple efficiency, work and power substitution.
questions.misconception: Applying efficiency in the wrong direction or treating weight as mass

explanation.body: The useful output power is $P_o=0.25P_i=0.25(10)=2.5\ \mathrm W$. The useful energy required is $E=mgh=20(0.50)=10\ \mathrm J$. Using $P_o=E/t$ gives $t=10/2.5=4.0\ \mathrm s$.

perOption.A: This time would require 250 W of useful power, far above the 2.5 W available.
perOption.B: This is the result of multiplying the ideal lifting time by the efficiency, which understates the time.
perOption.C: Correct. The motor delivers 10 J of useful work in 4.0 s.
perOption.D: This treats the load’s 20 N weight as a 20 kg mass and multiplies by gravitational acceleration again.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A mass $m$ is situated in space in a uniform gravitational field. [Diagram: horizontal parallel gravitational field lines; points P and Q on one line, Q a distance x to the right of P; no arrowheads shown on the field lines.] When the mass moves through a displacement $x$, from P to Q, it loses an amount of potential energy $E$. Which row correctly specifies the magnitude and the direction of the acceleration due to the gravity in this field? A $\dfrac{E}{x}$, → B $\dfrac{E}{x}$, ← C $\dfrac{E}{mx}$, → D $\dfrac{E}{mx}$, ←

stemImage.alt: Question 10: A mass m is situated in space in a uniform gravitational field. When the mass moves through a displacement x, from P to Q, it loses an amount of potential energ

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Relating loss of PE to work done by the field and the field direction.
questions.misconception: Confusing force (E/x) with field strength (E/mx), or reversing the field direction

explanation.body: In a uniform gravitational field, the potential energy lost over displacement $x$ along the field is $E=mgx$, giving $g=E/(mx)$. The field points towards lower gravitational potential, so the acceleration is from P to Q, to the right.

perOption.A: The quantity $E/x$ gives the gravitational force and must be divided by the mass.
perOption.B: The expression $E/x$ gives a force, and the leftward arrow points towards higher potential.
perOption.C: Correct. The acceleration points from P to Q.
perOption.D: The magnitude is right, but gravity points towards lower potential at Q.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The input power to the engine of a model car is 800 W. The efficiency of the engine is 40%.

The car travels at a constant velocity of 13 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ in a straight horizontal line.

What is the total horizontal resistive force on the car?
questions.stemText: The input power to the engine of a model car is 800 W. The efficiency of the engine is 40%. The car travels at a constant velocity of 13 m s–1 in a straight horizontal line. What is the total horizontal resistive force on the car? A 25 N B 37 N C 62 N D 150 N

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Efficiency then P = Fv with constant velocity.
questions.misconception: Using input power instead of useful output power

explanation.body: Using $P=Fv$ for the useful output power gives $0.40(800)=13F$, so the driving force is $24.6\ \mathrm{N}$. At constant velocity the driving and resistive forces balance, giving a resistive force of about $25\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the $60\%$ of power lost by the engine.
perOption.C: Uses all $800\ \mathrm{W}$ as useful output power.
perOption.D: Divides the input power by the efficiency before using $P=Fv$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A spring obeying Hooke's law has an unstretched length of 45 mm and a spring constant of $380\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. What is the increase in the elastic potential energy of the spring when its length increases from 50 mm to 60 mm? A 0.019 J B 0.038 J C 0.076 J D 0.21 J

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A spring obeying Hooke’s law has an unstretched length of 45 mm and a spring constant of 380 N m−1. What is the increase in the elastic potential energy of the

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must use extensions from natural length, not the change in length directly.
questions.misconception: Using the 10 mm change in length as the extension

explanation.body: The spring’s extension increases from $5\ \mathrm{mm}$ to $15\ \mathrm{mm}$. The increase in elastic potential energy is $\tfrac12 k(x_f^2-x_i^2)=\tfrac12(380)(0.015^2-0.005^2)=0.038\ \mathrm{J}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\tfrac12 k(\Delta x)^2$ instead of subtracting the initial energy from the final energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the factor of $\tfrac12$.
perOption.D: Uses the spring’s total lengths in place of its extensions.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A helicopter hovers stationary in mid-air. Its rotor blades sweep out a circular path of diameter D and push down a continuous column of air of density $\rho$ at a uniform speed v. The air above the blades is stationary. [Diagram: helicopter with rotor span D.] Which expression represents the average power P delivered to the air column by the blades? A $\frac{1}{8}\pi\rho D^2v^3$ B $\frac{1}{2}\pi\rho D^2v^3$ C $\frac{1}{4}\pi\rho D^2v^3$ D $\frac{1}{4}\pi\rho D^2v^2$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: A helicopter hovers stationary in mid-air. Its rotor blades sweep out a circular path of diameter D and push down a continuous column of air of density  at a u

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must model mass flow rate ρAv and the rate of KE transfer, with area from diameter.
questions.misconception: Using radius-diameter confusion or forgetting the ½ in kinetic energy

explanation.body: The rotor sweeps out area $A=\pi(D/2)^2=\pi D^2/4$, so the mass flow rate is $\Delta m/\Delta t=\rho Av$. The air starts at rest, so the rate of increase of its kinetic energy is $P=\tfrac12(\Delta m/\Delta t)v^2=\tfrac18\pi\rho D^2v^3$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the diameter as the radius when calculating the swept area.
perOption.C: Applies $P=Fv$ with the outgoing air speed and misses the factor of $\tfrac12$ in the kinetic energy.
perOption.D: Gives the force from the change in momentum per unit time instead of the power.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A body is accelerated from rest by a horizontal force F on a smooth surface through air. The magnitudes of F and air resistance R vary with displacement as shown. [Graph: force against displacement; F is an upper sloping straight line, R is a lower curve starting at zero; region P lies between F and R, region Q lies under R.] Which area represents the thermal energy dissipated? A P B Q C P − Q D P + Q

stemImage.alt: Question 7: A body is accelerated from rest by a horizontal force F on a smooth surface through air. The magnitudes of F and air resistance R vary with displacement as show

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Interpret area under a force–displacement graph as work done by each force.
questions.misconception: Confusing the gain in kinetic energy (P) with the energy dissipated

explanation.body: Thermal energy dissipated equals the work done against air resistance. This is the area under the force–displacement graph for $R$, which is region $Q$.

perOption.A: Uses the work done by the resultant force, which is the increase in kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Subtracts the resistance work from the net work, which already accounts for resistance.
perOption.D: Uses the total work done by the applied force, including the increase in kinetic energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
There are balanced forces acting on the steel ball when it is falling vertically in oil.

Which graph shows the variation with time of the gravitational potential energy $E_p$ and the kinetic energy $E_k$ of the ball?

[Four energy–time graphs:
A: $E_k$ is a horizontal line; $E_p$ is a straight line decreasing from above $E_k$.
B: $E_k$ is a horizontal line; $E_p$ is a curve decreasing at an increasing rate.
C: $E_k$ is a curve increasing from a non-zero value; $E_p$ is a curve decreasing at an increasing rate.
D: $E_k$ increases linearly from zero; $E_p$ decreases linearly to zero.]

stemImage.alt: Question 5: There are balanced forces acting on the steel ball when it is falling vertically in oil. Which graph shows the variation with time of the gravitational potentia

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: This needs a direct link from balanced forces to constant speed and a linear loss of $E_p$.
questions.misconception: Assuming gravitational potential energy is always converted into kinetic energy during a fall

explanation.body:
Since the resultant force on the ball is zero, it falls at constant velocity, so its kinetic energy stays constant with time.

Its height decreases at a constant rate, so its gravitational potential energy decreases linearly with time: $\dfrac{\Delta E_p}{t} = \dfrac{mgh}{t} = mgv$, so $\Delta E_p = (mgv)t$.

perOption.A: Correct. $E_k$ is constant and $E_p$ falls linearly.
perOption.B: $E_p$ is drawn falling at an increasing rate, which would need the ball to be speeding up.
perOption.C: $E_k$ is drawn increasing, which suggests the ball is accelerating even though the forces are balanced.
perOption.D: Treats the fall as if $E_p$ were converted into $E_k$, ignoring that the forces are balanced and the speed is constant.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A small boat is propelled by an engine and initially travels at a constant speed.

The resistive force acting on the boat is directly proportional to the square of its speed.

The power output of the engine is then reduced such that the driving force is reduced to half its original value. After some time, the boat reaches a new constant speed.

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{final power output}}{\text{initial power output}}$?

A. 0.125
B. 0.354
C. 0.500
D. 0.707

stemImage.alt: Question 5: A small boat is propelled by an engine and initially travels at a constant speed. The resistive force acting on the boat is directly proportional to the square

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires using force balance to find the speed ratio and then using the power relation.
questions.misconception: Assuming power scales directly with thrust as speed changes

explanation.body: At constant speed the driving force balances drag, so $F=kv^2$. Since $F_\mathrm{final}/F_\mathrm{initial}=1/2$, the speed ratio is $v_\mathrm{final}/v_\mathrm{initial}=1/\sqrt{2}$. Using $P=Fv=kv^3$, the power ratio is $(1/\sqrt{2})^3=0.354$.

perOption.A: Cubes $1/2$ as if the speed itself were halved.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses only the driving-force ratio and ignores the change in speed.
perOption.D: Uses the speed ratio alone and ignores the change in driving force.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A net force F acts on an object of mass m that is initially at rest. The object moves in a straight line. The variation of F with the distance s is shown.

What is the speed of the object at the distance s?
questions.stemText: A net force F acts on an object of mass m that is initially at rest. The object moves in a straight line. The variation of F with the distance s is shown. What is the speed of the object at the distance s? A $√F_{1}$$s_{1}$ 2m B $√F_{1}$$s_{1}$ m C $√2F_{1}$$s_{1}$ m D $√4F_{1}$$s_{1}$ m

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires reading a triangular area as net work and equating it to the gain in kinetic energy.
questions.misconception: Treating the force as constant

explanation.body: The area under the force–distance graph up to $s_1$ is the net work, $\tfrac12 F_1s_1$. The object starts at rest, so this work equals its final kinetic energy, $\tfrac12 mv^2$. Equating the two gives $v=\sqrt{F_1s_1/m}$.

perOption.A: Omits the factor of $\tfrac12$ in the kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the full rectangle $F_1s_1$ for work instead of the triangular area.
perOption.D: Overestimates the work by a factor of four compared with the triangular area.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A trolley runs from P to Q along a track. At Q its potential energy is 50 kJ less than at P.

At P, the kinetic energy of the trolley is 5 kJ. Between P and Q, the trolley does 10 kJ of work against friction.

What is the kinetic energy of the trolley at Q?
questions.stemText: A trolley runs from P to Q along a track. At Q its potential energy is 50 kJ less than at P. At P, the kinetic energy of the trolley is 5 kJ. Between P and Q, the trolley does 10 kJ of work against friction. What is the kinetic energy of the trolley at Q? A 35 kJ B 45 kJ C 55 kJ D 65 kJ

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires adding the initial energies and subtracting a single friction loss.
questions.misconception: Adding dissipated energy to kinetic energy

explanation.body: Set the potential energy at Q to zero, so the potential energy at P is $50\ \mathrm{kJ}$. The total energy at P is $50+5=55\ \mathrm{kJ}$. At Q, the energy balance is $55=0+K_Q+10$ in kilojoules, so $K_Q=45\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

perOption.A: Undercounts the final kinetic energy, for example by subtracting the friction loss twice.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Ignores the $10\ \mathrm{kJ}$ lost to friction.
perOption.D: Adds the work done against friction to the mechanical energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A car of mass 1400 kg is travelling on a straight, horizontal road at a constant speed of 25 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

The output power from the car’s engine is 30 kW.

The car then travels up a slope at 2° to the horizontal, maintaining the same constant speed.

What is the output power of the car’s engine when travelling up the slope?
questions.stemText: A car of mass 1400 kg is travelling on a straight, horizontal road at a constant speed of 25 m s–1. The output power from the car’s engine is 30 kW. The car then travels up a slope at 2° to the horizontal, maintaining the same constant speed. What is the output power of the car’s engine when travelling up the slope? A 12 kW B 31 kW C 42 kW D 65 kW

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires resolving weight along the slope, converting force into power and adding the original engine power.
questions.misconception: Confusing additional power with total power

explanation.body: The component of weight down the slope is $mg\sin 2^\circ=1400(9.81)\sin 2^\circ\approx479.3\ \mathrm{N}$. The extra power against gravity is $P_g=Fv=479.3(25)\approx12\ \mathrm{kW}$. Adding this to the original $30\ \mathrm{kW}$ gives $42\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the additional power needed against gravity.
perOption.B: Adds too little power for the downslope component of weight, which requires about $12\ \mathrm{kW}$.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Overestimates the additional power needed against gravity at this slope.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two identical balls were released simultaneously from rest at X and made their way to Y along two different tracks on the same vertical plane as shown in Fig. 7. Ball 1 travels along a straight down-slope track while ball 2 travels along a curve down-slope followed by an up-slope track. Ball 2 reaches Y first.

[Fig. 7 shows X above and to the left of Y. Track 1 is a dashed straight descent from X to Y. Track 2 is a solid curve that dips below Y before rising to it.]

Neglecting all resistive forces, what can be said of the final energy and the average rate of energy conversion for the two balls?

Final total energy | Higher average rate of energy conversion
A Both balls are the same | Ball 2
B Ball 2 is higher | Ball 1
C Ball 2 is higher | Ball 2
D Both balls are the same | Ball 1

stemImage.alt: Question 7: Two identical balls were released simultaneously from rest at X and made their way to Y along two different tracks on the same vertical plane as shown in Fig. 7

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires comparing conserved energy separately from energy converted per unit time.
questions.misconception: Confusing energy transferred with its rate of transfer

explanation.body: The balls start with equal total mechanical energy and there are no resistive forces, so their final total mechanical energies are equal. They undergo the same net energy conversion between X and Y, and ball 2 takes less time, so it has the higher average rate of conversion.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Assigns extra energy to ball 2 and credits the slower ball with the higher average rate.
perOption.C: Confuses ball 2’s higher rate of energy conversion with a higher final total energy.
perOption.D: Assigns the higher rate to the ball that takes longer to undergo the same net energy conversion.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The diagram shows a block P of mass $M$ connected by a string over a frictionless pulley to a block Q of mass $m$.

[P lies on an incline rising to the right at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The string runs up the incline over the pulley, then vertically down to Q.]

Block P moves up the slope with a constant velocity $v$. The slope is at angle $\theta$ to the horizontal. The acceleration of free fall is $g$.
The resistive forces on the blocks are negligible.
Which expressions gives the energy transferred per unit time to block P?

1. $mgv$
2. $Mgv\sin\theta$
3. $(M+m)gv$

A 1 and 2
B 1 only
C 2 and 3
D 2 only

stemImage.alt: Question 8: The diagram shows a block P of mass M connected by a string over a frictionless pulley to a block Q of mass m. Block P moves up the slope with a constant veloci

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires finding the same tension from two force balances and using it to calculate power.
questions.misconception: Adding the weights to compute the power delivered by the string

explanation.body: Let $T$ be the tension in the string. The blocks move at constant speed, so force balance gives $T=Mg\sin\theta=mg$. The rate at which the tension transfers energy to P is $Tv=Mgv\sin\theta=mgv$, so expressions 1 and 2 both apply.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Misses that the tension also equals the component of P’s weight along the slope.
perOption.C: Includes the sum of the weights and misses that Q’s weight equals the tension.
perOption.D: Misses that the tension equals the weight of Q.

A block of mass 5.0 kg is released from rest and slides down a ramp of horizontal length 2.0 m from an initial height of 1.0 m. A constant frictional force of 4.0 N acts on the block as it slides.

2.0 m

What is the speed of the block at the bottom of the ramp?
questions.stemText: A block of mass 5.0 kg is released from rest and slides down a ramp of horizontal length 2.0 m from an initial height of 1.0 m. A constant frictional force of 4.0 N acts on the block as it slides. block 1.0 m 2.0 m What is the speed of the block at the bottom of the ramp? A 4.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 4.4 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 16 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 40 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The ramp length must be calculated before frictional work can be included in the energy balance.
questions.misconception: Using horizontal distance for frictional work

explanation.body: The length of the slope is $s=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt{5}\ \mathrm{m}$. The energy balance is $\frac12mv^2=mgh-Fs$, so $\frac12(5)v^2=5(9.81)(1)-4\sqrt{5}$. This gives $v=4.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Ignores the energy dissipated by friction.
perOption.C: Reports the numerical value of $v^2$ as the speed.
perOption.D: Reports the numerical value of the final kinetic energy as the speed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A man pulls a rope attached to a sled. The rope makes an angle of $30^{\mathrm{o}}$ with the horizontal. The man exerts a force of 20.0 N on the rope to move the sled horizontally through a distance of 40 m.

What is the work done by the man?
questions.stemText: A man pulls a rope attached to a sled. The rope makes an angle of 30o with the horizontal. The man exerts a force of 20.0 N on the rope to move the sled horizontally through a distance of 40 m. What is the work done by the man? A 400 J B 490 J C 690 J D 800 J

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation uses the component of a given force along a given displacement.
questions.misconception: Using the full pulling force for horizontal work.

explanation.body: Work is the component of the pulling force along the sled’s motion multiplied by the distance moved. Thus $W=(20.0\cos 30^\circ)(40)\approx692.8\ \mathrm{J}$, which rounds to $690\ \mathrm{J}$ at the precision of the options.

perOption.A: Uses the vertical component $20.0sin30^circ$ for horizontal motion.
perOption.B: Uses an effective horizontal force of about $12.3 mathrm{N}$, below the actual $20.0cos30^circ$.
perOption.C: Correct. Only the horizontal force component does work on the sled.
perOption.D: Uses the full $20.0 mathrm{N}$ without projecting it along the displacement.

The graph below shows how the length L of a spring suspended from one end varies with the force F exerted on the other end.

Initially the spring has an extension of 2.5 cm. What is the work done to extend the spring by a
questions.stemText: The graph below shows how the length L of a spring suspended from one end varies with the force F exerted on the other end. L / cm 10.0 5.0 0 F / N 6.0 Initially the spring has an extension of 2.5 cm. What is the work done to extend the spring by a further 2.5 cm? A 0.11 J B 0.15 J C 0.26 J D 0.45 J

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must distinguish extension from total length and find the area against the correct axis.
questions.misconception: Treating length as extension or using the area against the force axis.

explanation.body: The spring length increases from $7.5$ to $10.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ while the force increases from $3.0$ to $6.0\ \mathrm{N}$. The work is the trapezoidal area between the line and the length axis over that interval. This gives $W=\tfrac12(3.0+6.0)(10.0-7.5)\times10^{-2}=0.11\ \mathrm{J}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct. The trapezoid uses the initial and final forces over the extra extension.
perOption.B: Uses the final force of 6.0 N throughout the extra extension.
perOption.C: Takes the area against the force axis using the mean length and the change in force.
perOption.D: Takes the entire trapezoid against the force axis from 0 to 6.0 N.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: An electric motor is required to haul a cage of mass 400 kg up a mine shaft through a vertical height of 1200 m in 2.0 minutes. What will be the electrical power required if the overall efficiency is 80%?
questions.stemText: An electric motor is required to haul a cage of mass 400 kg up a mine shaft through a vertical height of 1200 m in 2.0 minutes. What will be the electrical power required if the overall efficiency is 80%? A 3.2 kW B 4.9 kW C 32 kW D 49 kW

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting minutes to seconds and applying efficiency to the power balance.
questions.misconception: Multiplying useful power by efficiency.

explanation.body: The electrical input power multiplied by efficiency equals the gain in gravitational potential energy per unit time. Thus $P_\mathrm{in}=\frac{400\times9.81\times1200}{120}\div0.80=49\ \mathrm{kW}$.

perOption.A: Uses the efficiency factor in the wrong direction and is about a factor of ten below even that estimate.
perOption.B: Underestimates the correctly efficiency-adjusted power by a factor of ten.
perOption.C: Multiplies the useful power by efficiency instead of dividing.
perOption.D: Correct.
